extracted.intended_audience: systematic zoologists / taxonomists / naturalists concerned with zoological nomenclature and species description
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical principles for naming species and preparing systematic descriptions in zoology, including when to apply the law of priority, how to cite authors/references, and what constitutes adequate descriptive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority principle (law of priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of priority — the oldest available name should generally be the correct designation for a species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strickland defends priority as necessary for accuracy and for enabling others to judge dates and sources; Darwin recognises practical problems where strict application may do more harm than good (e.g., obscure earlier names that nobody would adopt). Guidance: apply priority generally, but be aware of cases where strict priority may cause confusion or inconvenience; consider a limited, rare break with priority only when adopting the earlier name would clearly be detrimental to scientific communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appending the first describer's name to a species
rubrics_metrics.description: Append the name of the first describer to a species name to indicate more precisely which taxon is meant and to furnish a clue to dates and original works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strickland: appending author names helps resolve misapplied names and locate original descriptions. Darwin objects that the practice encourages vanity and sloppy work; as a compromise, give a bibliographic reference (including author/date) in systematic works, and consider omitting the author's name from the binomial in non-systematic texts while still providing references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide at least one good reference (preferably a figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Append to the specific name ONE good reference to a standard work, especially to a FIGURE, with an accompanying synonym if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strickland recommends including a clear reference (even if cumbersome) because a single good reference or figure is far less harmful than uncertainty about identity. Use an explicit figure citation where possible so others can identify the taxon without ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, loose, and inadequate definitions of new species
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not describe new species with vague, loose, or inadequate descriptions that merely note a few prominent external characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin and Strickland both condemn 'mere naming' and 'wretched lines' as producing a large amount of bad work. Practical remedies suggested include public protest, community standards, and possibly a committee to 'write down the practice' and expose the worst examples to discourage careless descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit should follow thorough anatomical or systematic work, not mere naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit for taxonomic work should be due to those who work out species minutely and anatomically or who revise entire groups systematically; mere defining or naming without substantial work deserves little credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that mere naming is not comparable to serious scientific work and that incentives should favour careful anatomy and systematic revision. Incentives and recognition practices (e.g., not perpetually rewarding the first-to-name without rigour) should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not define species from single valves or small fragments alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Species (and hardly genera) should not be defined based on single valves or small portions that are highly variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin: describing a species from valves alone is akin to describing a crab from small portions of its carapace; such parts are highly variable and often insufficient. Collect and examine whole specimens and anatomical detail before erecting names based on fragmentary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult original specimens and original sources when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxonomists should, where practicable, consult original specimens and the original literature for reliable identification and dating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that he cannot recognise some species without the original specimen and that secondary compilations (e.g., Agassiz's dates) contain errors. Work should, when necessary, go back to type material and original descriptions to resolve synonymy and priority issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assigning names on the basis of plates or short descriptions alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying and naming species solely from plates or brief descriptions is unreliable and often amounts to guesswork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin points out that from plates or descriptions one can hardly determine British sessile cirripedes reliably. Taxonomists should not base new names or decisions on such guesswork; instead, seek specimens and detailed characters (including internal anatomy).

rubrics_metrics.name: When names are misapplied, append the author's name to clarify
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where the same specific name has been applied to different species (misapplied), append the author's name to indicate which author's concept is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strickland uses the example of Helix putris (Montagu vs Linnaeus): appending the author clarifies differing usages. Use author citations to disambiguate misapplied names in such contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer accurate but cumbersome referencing over uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to be cumbrous (e.g., by giving explicit references) than to leave species indications uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strickland accepts that giving a full reference (even if cumbersome) is preferable to ambiguity. Adopt explicit citation practices in systematic works to ensure clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-level reform and public standards to discourage poor descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The community should act (e.g., by a committee or congress) to classify modern works by merit and to formally protest vague definitions, thereby discouraging careless 'species-mongering'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strickland suggests a committee to prepare a 'CLASS LIST' of works arranged by merit, exposing the worst examples 'in terrorem'. He also mentions that a congress of scientific bodies could help resolve nomenclatural chaos. Practical community action and public standards are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow rare exceptions to strict priority for convenience and high merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where strict application of priority would replace a well-known name worldwide with an obscure earlier name, consider rare exceptions favouring convenience and scientific merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that forcing adoption of obscure resurrected names (which will not be followed) could do more harm than good; in such cases he contemplates rejecting strict priority. Any exception should be rare and weighed against the usefulness of stability and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer references (including author/date) without permanently appending author to binomial in non-systematic works
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a bibliographic reference to the first describer (author/date/source) without necessarily making the author's name part of the binomial for ordinary usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin proposes that systematic works should include historical references, but in non-systematic contexts a reference (e.g., 'Lam. An. Invert., etc.') rather than appending 'mihi' or an author's name to the binomial may curb vanity while preserving traceability.
